 Here are Social Security's 2027 maximum taxable earnings
 Kerry Hannon · Senior Columnist Wed, November 4, 2026 at 7:28 AM PST 3 min read When the Social Security Administration announced its annual cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, the program also released new income thresholds subject to payroll taxes next year. 
 Social Security benefits are funded through payroll taxes, which are then invested in trust funds and paid out in monthly checks to millions of retirees and people with disabilities. 
 The tax only applies to earnings up to a yearly cap. Next year, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax in 2027 will jump to $192,300, up from $184,500 this year. 
 Here's how the math breaks down: Workers and their employers each pay 6.2% on wages up to that amount. If you're self-employed, you pay the entire amount — 12.4%.  
 That means the maximum Social Security withholding for a worker next year will be $23,842, or 12.4% of $192,300. Any income above that amount is not subject to the Social Security tax.   
 That's where things get sticky. 
 Read more: Social Security COLA for 2027: How to find out how much more you'll get 
 A deeper dive into the payroll tax 
 The backdrop: Social Security's reserves could run out at the end of 2032. At that point, if no adjustments are made, the entitlement program's Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will be able to pay out only about 80% of benefits to seniors, according to the 2026 Social Security and Medicare Trustees' annual report. 
 Raising that earnings tax cap, or eliminating it, has been a contentious debate in Washington in addressing the future of Social Security. 
 Read more:  Retirement planning by age: The complete guide for your 20s-70s 
 Lawmakers have floated a range of fixes, from raising payroll taxes to increasing the retirement age for younger workers to lifting the cap on earnings subject to Social Security taxes. 
 "Congress has only two options to address the projected shortfall," Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance. "Bring more money into Social Security, or cut benefits." 
 The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% increase in benefits for 2027, the largest adjustment since 2023, providing roughly 76 million Americans with higher payments to help offset rising living costs. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) · Andrew Harnik via Getty Images One proposal that has attracted bipartisan attention: Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio have introduced legislation to eliminate the income cap on Social Security contributions. 
 As they wrote in a New York Times op-ed in July: "This is a no-brainer: The wealthiest Americans, who have benefited the most from America's opportunities, should contribute the same percentage of their income as a factory worker in Chillicothe, Ohio, or a teacher in Worcester, Mass." 
 Story Continues Read more:  How much do you really need to save for retirement? 
 More than 6 in 10 Americans worry Social Security won't be available throughout their retirement, according to the Allianz Center for the Future of Retirement. 
 "Social Security's future is on the ballot this November," Altman said. "With the shortfall being projected within the next six years, anybody elected to the Senate will be in office, likely voting on that legislation to reform Social Security.  
 "If Congress does not act, for many retirees, if their income drops by 20%, that's catastrophic," she added.

She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich."
